title: Study Plan and Readiness
oneLiner: A plan through what a big-tech loop covers, shaped by your level, target role and weekly hours, and a view of the evidence for each area.
keyTakeaway: Interview prep goes wrong in two ways: spending weeks on the topics you already like, and leaving system design and behavioral stories to the last few days. A plan that interleaves all four areas, and a regular look at where you're weakest, fixes both.
explanation:
A typical big-tech loop has two or three coding rounds, one or two system design rounds (one for junior roles, sometimes swapped for an object-oriented design round), and a behavioral round, which at Amazon is woven into every interview. The plan covers all of them in five phases: foundations, core data structures, graphs and heaps, dynamic programming with design depth, and a final phase of timed mock interviews. System design starts in phase two and behavioral stories in week one, so neither is crammed at the end. Concurrency, memory, design patterns, operating systems, testing and AI lessons run alongside, with short pattern quiz and glossary flash card sessions recurring through the weeks.

Not everyone needs the same plan, so it asks three things. Where you start: someone new to programming gets a prerequisites block first and the hardest topics marked optional, while an experienced engineer gets the easy warm-ups turned into optional checks. What the interviews are for: a backend target adds databases and more design walk-throughs and trims niche algorithms, and a senior, design heavy target moves system design earlier and adds repeat walk-throughs and extra behavioral rounds. And how many hours a week you really have, which decides how many weeks the core material takes. Optional material is listed with a reason but not scheduled, each phase says what it needs before you start it, and a slack week after every four weeks (plus one at the end) is kept free for failed attempts, revision and repeat mocks. Lessons tick themselves off when you pass them, design walk-throughs when you've compared every stage, story-bank goals when you have enough stories, and pattern quiz runs when you finish them. Tick everything else yourself.

The readiness tab keeps four kinds of evidence apart instead of blending them into one percentage. Coverage: lessons you have opened or run, walk-throughs started, story themes covered. Assisted practice: coding lessons passed from the guided starter or soon after opening the reference solution, and the points you ticked yourself against a model answer. Independent: coding lessons passed from the bare starter with no reference in the week before, and quiz and flash card results where the answer was hidden. Timed: problems solved in the mixed interview set and behavioral mock rounds. Each figure names what produced it, and where nothing measures a kind (nothing here can judge a design you produced alone) it says so. It's a guide to what to practise next, not a prediction of the outcome. The "Focus next" list links straight to the most useful next step, such as redoing an assisted pass from the bare starter.

Your plan and practice history are kept in this browser. Lesson progress is on the server as usual.

Not preparing for a big-tech interview? Switch to the second path at the top, Well-rounded IT & CS: the same plan and progress views over a broad route through hardware, programming, operating systems, networking, security, Linux, databases, Git, system design basics and AI. Each path keeps its own plan.
